claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA contains a dual-nanoprecipitation microstructure.
Additive manufacturing produces a refined, non-equilibrium nanostructure in this alloy.
Nanoprecipitates in the alloy can serve as preferential sites for oxygen accumulation.
Nanoprecipitate interfaces enhance elemental segregation during oxidation.
Oxygen diffuses into the alloy during high-temperature oxidation.
Oxygen preferentially segregates at nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces.
Localized oxygen enrichment at nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces promotes adherent, self-healing oxide layers.
The proposed protective oxide layers may be enriched in Cr and Ti.
The proposed oxide layers act as diffusion barriers.
The diffusion-barrier effect slows further oxidation of the underlying matrix.
APT will reveal distinct oxygen enrichment at nanoprecipitate interfaces in the additively manufactured alloy.
Interfacial oxygen-enriched regions will correspond to zones of protective oxide formation.
The additively manufactured alloy will exhibit reduced oxidation weight gain relative to cast or wrought material of the same composition.
The additively manufactured alloy will develop thinner oxide scales than cast or wrought material of the same composition.
Cast or wrought material has a less pronounced nanoprecipitate distribution and less interfacial segregation than the additively manufactured alloy.
At higher temperatures or longer exposure times, oxide-scale spallation or nanoprecipitate coarsening may weaken the protective effect.
Processing-induced residual stresses and minor alloying elements may influence oxidation behavior.
APT can be used as a microstructural characterization method in precipitation-containing high-entropy alloys.
Weight-change measurements under high-temperature air exposure can be used to examine oxidation behavior.
